title: The golden rule (Matthew 7:12)
hookLine: do to others what you'd want done to you
last: ASK, AND IT SHALL BE GIVEN.

cards: It turns up on classroom posters, in a grandparent's advice, after a shove between siblings. Treat people the way you want to be treated. It sounds so much like common sense that it can seem to have no author at all.
But it has an address: near the end of the Sermon on the Mount, one verse long, standing on its own like a signpost. And Jesus says something big about it: this one line is the law and the prophets.

teach.h: NEVER CALLED GOLDEN IN THE BIBLE.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets." Three things to notice. First, the name.
The Bible never calls it golden; that label came along much later, in English. Second, the ending.

The law and the prophets was how people in Jesus's time named their scriptures, the teachings of Moses and the writings of the prophets. So if you want the heart of the scriptures in one sentence, here it is.
Third, it's phrased as something to do: what you'd love someone to do for you, go and do it first. Jesus wasn't the only teacher who found the whole of scripture in one line.
The Talmud tells of the sage Hillel, who was challenged to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot.

He answered that what is hateful to you, you shouldn't do to your neighbor; that is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary, now go and learn it. His version names what not to do; Jesus's names what to do.

The Book of Tobit has a similar saying. Leviticus holds the root of all of them: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Christians often read the golden rule as that commandment turned into a daily test.
The ordinary-Tuesday version: before you text, before you reply, before you walk past, flip the seats. If I were them right now, what would I hope for? Then do that.

how: Christian parents often teach the golden rule to children as a first rule of life, and some use it as a quick test before acting: if I were them, what would I hope for?

games.q: you're about to reply to a message that annoyed you. what does the golden rule ask you to do first?
o: flip the seats: what would I hope for if I were them?
games.why: "all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them." the rule starts with imagining their side.

practice: Think of one small thing you'd love someone to do for you this week: a text that says I'm thinking of you, a coffee left on your desk, the trash taken out without being asked. Hold it for a moment.
Then think of one person who might love the same thing, and picture doing it for them.
